subject: Reserved Capacity: fallback playbook & queueing behavior for Centaur Health

Cc: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.ai>
Date: Tue, 18 May 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Reserved Capacity: fallback playbook & queueing behavior for Centaur Health

Hi Erin —

Thanks again for the time yesterday. Per our call, Centaur Health is interested in a Dedicated (reserved) GPU pool with deterministic throughput for your inference service. A couple of items came up that Procurement and your SRE team asked us to put in writing so they can evaluate the SOW:

- What happens when the reserved pool is saturated (e.g., live traffic spike)? Will Centaur requests be queued, or do we preempt best-effort workloads?
- Tail-latency guarantees and what controls trigger fallbacks to a hosted/compatible model variant.
- How credits or remediation work if throughput SLAs are not met during maintenance windows or regional outages.

Attached is an initial draft of a simple "fallback playbook" that lays out the high-level steps and decision points (capacity-fallback-playbook-v1.pdf). Can you confirm if this is the kind of doc Procurement wants, and whether we should expand with a short technical appendix for your SREs?

Next steps I propose:
1) You confirm requirements from Procurement/SRE (bandwidth, tail latency target, preferred fallback model).
2) We map these to carve-outs (burst buffer size, preemption thresholds).
3) Diego will produce a short tech appendix on queueing and preemption for the SOW.

I'll hold off on the formal SOW until we capture these items.

Thanks —
Ben

Subject: Re: Reserved Capacity: fallback playbook & queueing behavior for Centaur Health

Thanks Ben — appreciate the draft. A few clarifying questions from our side so Procurement and SRE can sign off:

1) Throughput guarantees: we need to understand the guaranteed tokens/sec per tenant under peak conditions and what percentage of the pool can be reserved for bursts. Our target is to avoid tail-latency spikes above 200ms P95 for text-generation workloads.

2) Queueing behavior: when you say "queueing" are requests buffered (in memory) or do you return an immediate 429/503? We need to know how long requests will wait before being rejected.

3) Preemption policy: if you preempt best-effort jobs to honor reserved capacity, what is the observable behavior on our side (errors, increased queuing) and how long does preemption take?

4) Credits/remediation: what is the proposed SLA crediting formula for dedicated pool availability breaches? A simple example would help.

If you can answer these at a high level, Procurement will mark the SOW as "ready for review". We can loop in our SRE (Jared) if you want to get into queueing knobs.

—Erin

Erin — thanks for the clear list. Happy to outline what we normally include in an enterprise SOW appendix and the playbook language. High level answers below, followed by proposed next steps. Diego, please review the technical bullets and add anything I missed.

High level (executive-friendly):
- Guaranteed throughput: we map reserved GPUs to a nominal tokens/sec profile per model class. For example, a 2xA10-equivalent reserved node maps to ~2.5k tokens/sec for small-context generation (your workloads will vary depending on prompt length). The SOW will include a table with nominal throughput per node and an aggregate guaranteed floor.
- Queueing vs immediate rejection: our platform will queue up to a configurable per-tenant backlog for a short duration (default 30s) before returning a 429. We can shorten/lengthen for Centaur during onboarding.
- Preemption: reserved capacity preempts best-effort workloads within the local host pool. Preemption is near-instant at scheduling time; client-side you will see increased queue time for best-effort requests followed by 429s if the backlog exceeds threshold.
- Credits: standard model is pro-rata credits based on the fraction of time the reserved pool is below the guaranteed throughput. We can provide an example formula in the SOW.

Next steps proposed:
1) Diego will draft a short technical appendix (queueing thresholds, backlog sizing, preemption steps) and a diagram for your SREs.
2) We provide a small test run in a staging window to exercise preemption and measure tail-latency.
3) Formalize SLO crediting example in SOW.

Diego — can you attach a simple diagram of host-level queueing and a quick note on KV-cache impact on tail-latency? Ben, I can prep the SOW appendix after Diego's note.

Thanks,

Lauren, Ben — quick technical appendix below. Erin — tagging the answers to your numbered questions inline, and attaching a diagram (queueing-behavior-diagram.svg).

--- Technical appendix (summary) ---
1) Throughput guarantees
- How we define it: guaranteed throughput = sum of per-node nominal throughput across the reserved pool. Nominal throughput numbers are model- and context-length dependent; we will profile Centaur's primary model and include a table in the SOW.
- Safeguards: we reserve a small headroom (default 7%) to reduce oscillation during short spikes; this is configurable.

2) Queueing behavior (your question on buffering vs immediate rejection)
- Short buffering: requests enter an in-memory queue at the local serving host and are eligible for immediate scheduling when a slot frees.
- Backlog sizing: default per-tenant backlog = 30s of expected processing time (configurable). After backlog timeout is hit we return 429 to the caller.
- Visibility: we emit a metric (tenant.queue_depth, tenant.mean_wait_ms) and traces for requests that exceed 10ms wait so your SREs can correlate tail latency.

3) Preemption policy
- Mechanism: reserved requests get priority in the scheduler. Best-effort tasks are evicted preferentially from the local queue or preempted after a grace period (usually <200ms).
- Observability: on preemption you will see immediate increase in queue_depth for preempted tenants and a short window of elevated retry rates. Preemptions are logged and surfaced to the console.

4) Credits / remediation example
- Simple formula (example for inclusion in SOW): credit = committed_monthly_fee * min(1, (1 - (actual_up_time / committed_uptime_target))).
- Example: If committed uptime is 99.9% for the month but measured is 99.7%, credit = monthly_fee * (1 - 0.997/0.999) ≈ monthly_fee * 0.002002. We will agree on a measurement methodology in the SOW (time-window, exclusions for force-majeure/maintenance).

Additional notes:
- KV-cache warm starts: cold KV caches can add latency on long-form generation; we recommend enabling prefix caching for recurrent prompts. Cache warm thresholds and eviction policies are part of the appendix.
- Burst behavior: we support a short-duration burst pool that can be consumed concurrently; bursts are gated by burst tokens and can be capped per-customer to avoid noisy neighbors.

Attachment: queueing-behavior-diagram.svg (illustrates per-host queues, preemption flow, and backlog timeout)

Erin — if this looks reasonable I will: (a) expand the appendix to a 2-page SRE note, (b) prepare a short staging test plan (30m window, synthetic spike), and (c) add a sample SLO credit table for the SOW.

Ben — happy to draft the diagrams and the staging test harness next.

—Diego
